Read the following passage and then answer questions 1 to 5.

Many people do not have enough time to rest adequately. However, it is important to prioritise
rest and quality sleep every day. Rest and sleep are two different things, but both are equally important
for our mental, emotional and physical health. Actually, prioritising rest can improve one’s quality of
sleep.

Rest can be difficult to define because it can mean different things to different people. It can be
active, such as going for a walk outside, or passive, such as taking a moment to sit down and breathe
deeply. Regardless of how you choose to rest, these actions can help you recover and recharge from
physical and mental effort. That is why quality rest is linked to improved physical and mental health.

Sleep on the other hand is a state in which individuals are mentally detached from their
surroundings. It is an essential part of the body’s well being. Quality sleep can help us to reset, recover
and recharge our bodies. Unlike rest, sleep is something the body cannot function without. In fact, if
you are deprived of sleep, your body will force you to sleep, no matter what you are in the middle of
doing,

Read the following passage and then answer questions 6 to 10.

Laughter is normally an expression of happiness. This is probably because when we laugh, our
faces brighten up. We generally laugh when we are amused. When we hear a joke, the natural response
is to let out a laugh. However, not all people laugh at the same things. What one person finds amusing
may be ordinary or even unpleasant to another.

Laughter is not always a sign of delight. Most of us have, without doubt, seen people laughing
when there is nothing really funny. Such laughter could be out of nervousness or even politeness. A
saying goes, “A rich man’s joke is always funny”. This means people are expected to laugh when a person
of high status cracks a joke, however flat. Sometimes people laugh to mock others with the intention of
making the victim feel bad. Such derisive laughter is unfortunate. Genuine laughter is thought to be
healthy. No wonder, someone said that laughter is the best medicine.

Read the following passage and then answer questions 11 to 16.

When the headteacher, Mr. Mutandi walked into our classroom carrying a book and two medium-
sized sticks, the class went dead silent. We had never seen our headteacher walk around with sticks
Earlier in the day during the morning assembly, he had warned us against sneaking mobile phones into
school. “It is an offence for learners to have phones in school. Anybody found with one will face dire
consequences,” Mr. Mutandi had emphasised.

We were therefore worried when the headteacher came to class carrying the sticks. “Who could
be having a phone? When was he or she found? Where was the phone?” These were the questions
running through our minds. Mr. Mutandi placed the sticks on the table and opened the book. Mwajuma,
one of the girls in the class swiftly stood up.

“Sir, please forgive the offender,” she said. The headteacher looked surprised. “What is it,
Mwajuma? Who do I forgive?” He inquired. “The person who came with the phone,” Mwajuma said
in a trembling voice. “Oh, did someone come to school with a phone? And after the warnings I gave?”
There was pin-drop silence in the room

“Anyway, we will handle that after our lesson today. I am standing in for your Creative Arts
teacher, Madam Sitati, who is unwell. And these two sticks will be used to demonstrate how we can
make a sailing boat using material available in our immediate environment. Now get your exercise books
out.” We smiled at one another. All of us were ready for the lesson.
